method.p: For each company, take its percentile rank among the 42 on total assets, on revenue and on net profit, from the latest full-year figures found (FY2025 where published). Where a company has published nothing newer, its latest published year is used and shown next to the figure: Agrinas Pangan (Yodya Karya's 2020 and 2022 figures), Peruri (2023). The finance score is 5 times the average of those percentiles, using at least two of the three. For banks, revenue means operating income.
method.f: finance = 5 × mean( pct(assets), pct(revenue), pct(net profit) )

method.p: Money the company earns from its own customers: 5 times the average of its percentile ranks on revenue and on net profit. Assets are left out, so a large balance sheet built with state money does not count here.

Average of two 0–5 bands from the responsibility research: public money flowing through the company each year (subsidies, PSO, compensation, pensions, state-repaid programme debt) and state-backed debt it carries (money the state owes it, state-repaid or guaranteed programme loans, rescue liabilities). Bands: public money 1 = under Rp1T, 2 = Rp1–5T, 3 = Rp5–25T, 4 = Rp25–100T, 5 = over Rp100T a year; state-backed debt 1 = under Rp5T, 2 = Rp5–25T, 3 = Rp25–100T, 4 = Rp100–250T, 5 = over Rp250T.
Average of the balance-sheet score, the public-money band and the state-backed-debt band, so a new company carrying a large state programme counts alongside an established one with big accounts.
The reach band from the responsibility research: people or customers served by the public duty. 1 = under 1 million, 2 = 1–5 million, 3 = 5–20 million, 4 = 20–60 million, 5 = over 60 million.

0–5: formal instruments that name the company (0–2), plus its role in the President's flagship programmes (0–2), plus direct presidential attention in 2025–26 (0–1). A company with a standing public-service mandate gets at least 1.
0–5: how critical the sector is (0–2), plus a sole or statutory mandate (0–2), plus economy-wide or banking-system scale (0–1).

0–5, weighted: 0.30 × public money handled (subsidies, PSO, compensation, state-repaid programme debt) + 0.30 × people served + 0.15 × how essential and exclusive the mandate is + 0.25 × state exposure.

Sum of five parts, floored at 0: global company rankings such as Fortune and Forbes (up to 1.25), employer rankings such as LinkedIn Top Companies and Forbes World's Best Employers (up to 1.5), brand value from Brand Finance (up to 1.25), LinkedIn followers (up to 1), minus penalties for documented scandals or heavy losses (up to 1).

0–5, higher means more trouble, added up from four parts: legal exposure (up to 3; seniority of the people implicated, size of the alleged loss, several cases or a 2026 step; an allegation without a formal case counts at reduced weight), financial distress such as restructuring, negative equity or a state rescue (up to 1), audit and governance red flags such as BPK findings (up to 0.5), and a change of president director in 2025–26 (up to 0.5). Cases run from 2023 to October 2026.

list: A dash means nothing public was found during the research. It does not mean zero.
A shared web-search budget ran out partway through the research, so some pages were fetched directly and some gaps remain.
The five rubric scores are judgment applied to public evidence. Each one carries a one-line reason and a source in the company's card.
Ranks marked = are shared with other companies on the same score.

BUMN paid Rp131.41 trillion in dividends to Danantara in 2025, from 2024 profits. Pertamina paid the most, Rp42.10 trillion, followed by Bank Mandiri and MIND ID.
Danantara is cutting about 1,046 BUMN entities to roughly 200 core companies by the end of 2026.
